Quadratic cones, point sources and vertex directions

Exposition and figure: GPT-6 Astra (OpenAI), October 2026. Original exposition: CC0. Supplied programme readings retain their stated credits and licences.

A quadratic cone is smooth away from its vertex. There, its singular directions come from a one-dimensional boundary value. At the vertex a point source can force every direction to be singular, whereas a homogeneous equation permits only characteristic directions. The signature determines which of these two mechanisms governs a normalized one-sided power. More general holomorphic boundary values also admit moving smooth arguments, with a precise distinction between regular and critical limiting maps.

We use the complete boundary-power construction in Complex powers at a boundary, Lemma 1.1, Proposition 1.2, Theorem 2.1, Proposition 3.1, Corollary 3.2 and Theorem 4.1. Homogeneous extensions and angular moments, Theorems 1.2–3.1, constructs the angular representation and the unique continuous nonresonant extension. Point sources and complex Gaussian kernels, Theorem 1.1 and Lemma 2.1, proves the Laplacian source constants, symmetric diagonalization and the determinant branch. The parameter estimates and holomorphic identity argument are also developed in Complex quadratic powers and the Cauchy kernel, Section 1.

The supplied smooth pullback reading, Sections 18.1–18.5, proves ordinary wavefront localization, coordinate covariance and the exact submersion converse, especially (WF12)–(WF15). Its coordinate completion is Regular level sets and transverse convolution, Lemma 0.2. Cones and derivative-growth wavefronts, Theorem 6, proves ; Analytic equations and characteristic directions, Theorem 3 and its preceding finite transpose construction, proves analytic regularity outside the characteristic set. The Fourier, Gamma and angular foundations supply the integrals, recurrence and sphere measure used below.

All wavefront sets in the conclusions of this lesson are ordinary smooth wavefront sets. Fourier transformation uses . Pairings are complex bilinear.

Lemma 1 (scalar wavefronts). For every real , For every real ,

Proof. Corollary 3.2 of the boundary-power reading gives The exponent at zero is greater than . For a compact smooth cutoff , the product-transform formula gives an absolutely convergent convolution with . If , its absolute value is at most The last integral follows by ; it is finite for . Taking arbitrarily large excludes every negative direction. The distribution is smooth away from zero. It is not smooth at zero, since on it equals , which is unbounded as . The ordinary wavefront projection theorem therefore supplies a direction at zero; conicity leaves exactly the positive ray. Complex conjugation gives the negative ray for .

For the logarithm, choose near zero. Theorem 4.1 of that reading gives The second term is smooth and compactly supported, since vanishes near zero. The first has rapid Fourier decrease on the negative ray by the preceding calculation. Fourier differentiation and division by there give the same decrease for . Its unbounded logarithm at zero supplies the positive ray. Conjugation again gives the lower sign.

Each is real, supported in , smooth away from zero and nonzero. At a negative integer it is a nonzero delta derivative. At every other real parameter it has the nonzero density on . If it were smooth at zero, its vanishing on the negative side would force every Taylor coefficient there to vanish. Taylor's estimate of order , compared with that density as , is impossible. A nonzero delta derivative is also not smooth: a continuous function supported at a point is zero. Thus zero is its singular base point. For a real cutoff and a real distribution, the Fourier values in opposite directions are complex conjugates. Regularity in one ray is consequently equivalent to regularity in the other. Projection and conicity give both rays. Reflection proves the assertion for .

Proof. For , the exact linear chain rule gives , and . Iteration proves the displayed source identity, with the factor retained for every . Boundary values along arbitrary smooth approaches

The boundary limit also survives a moving complex argument. The hypotheses concern its real limiting map and its convergence in the smooth topology; the height need not be proportional to the parameter, and the real part may move.

We use Cauchy kernels and distributional boundary limits, Theorem 3.1 and Corollary 3.2, for the horizontal boundary distribution on finite-regularity tests. Gluing holomorphic sides, Lemma 1.1, constructs an -fold primitive with logarithmic growth. The exact submersion construction is the supplied smooth pullback reading, Section 18.5; its completed coordinates and Jacobian are supplied by the coordinate-completion lemma cited at the start of this lesson.

Let be an open interval, let , and set Let be holomorphic on . On each compact interval , assume a bound where is a nonnegative integer and . Larger compact intervals may require larger integers. These local bounds give the boundary distribution .

Continuity of that limit and the same uniform estimate prove joint continuity at the real boundary.

Proof in completed coordinates. Since , complete to coordinates in a neighborhood of any point. Use a compactly supported local test and a slightly larger such chart. Replace by its expression in these coordinates; it converges to in every smooth seminorm. The test becomes The absolute Jacobian is essential. It is smooth and positive on this chart. Every test derivative through any fixed order is bounded by a constant times the corresponding finite norm of , by the product and chain rules. Its support lies in one fixed compact set.

The real projections of of that compact set lie in one retained interval for small , and their imaginary parts tend uniformly to zero from above. Choose the continuous primitive of Lemma 7 on a larger rectangle, and write . The transpose is bilinear: there is no complex conjugation of .

The complex chain rule gives . After integrations by parts, Only is integrated by parts, and compact support removes each end term.

Here are estimates uniform in the test. Expanding the finite product of first-order operators gives To justify these expansions, start from . An induction writes its -th power as a sum of derivatives , , with coefficients that are finite sums of products of derivatives of through order . Differentiating once and using the product rule proves the next step. All coefficients are uniformly bounded on the fixed support, and converge to those of , because in . Multiplying their supremum bounds by the finite support volume proves (A14).

Localization and the test topology. Cover by finitely many such charts and use a fixed smooth partition. If their growth exponents differ, take the largest of their finite test orders. Each partition multiplier and coordinate change is continuous in that finite norm. Summing (A15) gives the first estimate in (A10); boundedness of , (A14), and the corresponding limit integral give the second. The submersion pullbacks agree on overlaps by their proved coordinate construction, so the limit is on all of .

The same formulas extend continuously to tests with fixed support, by the supplied finite-norm smoothing approximation; equivalently one may integrate by parts directly for those tests. If in with common support, the common bound controls the pairing with , and the fixed-test difference tends to zero by (A10). A bounded smooth test set has a common compact support and bounded norm, so (A10) proves strong distributional convergence. For the lower side apply the upper theorem to , the maps , and the submersion . Reflection and the already proved pullback composition law identify the limit with .

No estimate of the form occurs in this proof. In particular, a jointly smooth map with , nonzero , and positive-height values satisfies (A8) on each compact set and therefore (A9). This includes arbitrary smooth real drift and heights flat at .

Corollary 9 (critical points over regular boundary values). Retain the hypotheses on and , but allow at some points. Suppose that at every such point , extends holomorphically to a complex neighborhood of , agreeing with its original values above the interval. Then still has a distributional limit. Near regular points it is the submersion pullback of Theorem 8; near each critical point it is the smooth function given by the holomorphic extension composed with .

Proof. Around a critical point, shrink the source neighborhood so that the image of its closure under lies in a compact subset of the extension domain. For small , its image under remains in that domain. Uniform continuity of each derivative of the extension on a slightly larger compact set, together with the finite chain rule and (A8), gives convergence in every smooth seminorm to the extension composed with . Around regular points Theorem 8 applies. On an overlap the local distributional limits coincide, since they are limits of the same functions against every test there. A finite partition on each compact support therefore defines the global limit, with the local finite-test estimates already proved. This argument asserts no pullback at a critical point lying over a singular boundary value.

Exercise 6 (foundation: a height flatter than every power). For , set Determine the distributional limit of . Determine also the limit when the sign of the imaginary part is reversed, and for the upper approach with limiting real map .

Solution. The imaginary part in (A17) is positive. On each compact set every -derivative of tends to zero; thus (A8) holds with . Theorem 8 and the previously proved pole limits give For a fixed strip height , the maps lie in that strip when . Reversing the imaginary sign gives .

The height has no positive lower bound by , for any fixed and . Indeed, with , the quantity tends to zero: choose an integer in . Defining the exponential factor to be zero at gives a smooth function there. Repeated differentiation for has the form a polynomial in times ; the same bound makes each derivative tend to zero, and the fundamental theorem successively identifies the extensions as derivatives at zero. Hence this is also a jointly smooth approach, with all height derivatives zero at the boundary.

For the upper approach , the limiting map is reflection. The scalar identity , , gives The delta coefficient retains its sign because scalar distributional pullback uses the absolute Jacobian. The same result follows by reflection in Theorem 8.

Exercise 7 (intermediate: two simple level zeros and one harmless critical point). Let Find the distributional limit of on the whole real line, including and the two roots of the limiting real map.

Solution. The maps approach in the smooth topology. Their positive heights are at most . The sole critical point of is zero, whose image is ; the function is holomorphic near that image. Corollary 9 therefore applies at zero, giving the ordinary smooth limit there. At each of the roots , , so Theorem 8 and the pole formula apply. They give

Here are the real principal-value and density factors explicitly. The pulled-back delta has coefficient at each root, by the one-dimensional change-of-variables test formula. The pulled-back principal value is the limit of . To identify it, use Near , write , so . The endpoints removed by satisfy . This follows directly by solving the two quadratic equations, or by Taylor's formula for their local inverse, whose derivative has magnitude . Replacing these endpoints by the symmetric endpoints changes the singular integral by : the endpoint differences have length , and the integrand has size on those small intervals. The remaining local term is bounded. Thus the level-deletion limit is exactly the displayed combination of ordinary principal values. Away from the two roots it is the ordinary function. These local descriptions agree on overlaps and establish (A21) globally, without treating the critical point over as a singular level.

Exercise 8 (advanced: concentration at a critical singular level). Show that the smooth upper approach does not give a distributional limit for . Explain why this does not assert failure for every holomorphic at every critical map.

Solution. Choose a nonnegative compact smooth test , equal to one on , . Direct algebra gives For and , the denominator is at most . Hence A distributional limit would have a finite limit on this one fixed test, so it cannot exist. Both the nonzero-derivative hypothesis of Theorem 8 and the holomorphic-extension condition at the critical image in Corollary 9 fail at zero. The figure shows the exact concentration profiles in (A22); the inequality above proves the divergence for every sufficiently small parameter, independently of those samples.

For contrast within this same calculation, has no singular boundary value: smoothly, although the limiting map remains critical at zero. Thus the submersion condition is sufficient for all the admitted boundary functions, and cannot simply be dropped for that entire class; it is not necessary for each individual regular function.
